title: AI Detection Isn't About Style, It's About Information Inflation
dek: The tell of AI writing isn't style but the 'information inflation' where output exceeds input. A hedge fund titan's public admission about his AI-written op-ed became a turning point—Pangram's fourth generation has a false positive rate of about 1 in 24,000, and the more models converge, the easier they are to catch.
why: The CEO himself breaks down the classifier's principles, how training data is constructed, and the false positive rate metrics, while also debunking the astroturfing behind online 'false positive' complaints. For decision-makers judging the authenticity of AI writing, this is information-dense.
who: Product and technology leads working on content moderation, recruitment screening, and academic integrity, as well as content teams that heavily use LLMs to produce text and need to know where the boundaries lie.
skip: The Shell Game podcast and philosophical digression from 53:00-57:00 can be skipped without missing the main thread.

points.h: 'Did you use AI?' is the wrong question; ask where the ideas came from
points.body: Event: Stanley Druckenmiller published an op-ed in the WSJ that was clearly AI-written; someone ran it through Pangram and got a 100% AI score. The turning point was that he didn't hide it—he admitted, 'I'm essentially not a good writer, I just used AI,' and the WSJ refused to retract it. Bryan pushed further: since he admitted it, show the prompt. 'Did you use AI?' is a false binary; the real question is where the ideas came from—whether it's 'help me write an op-ed against the Treasury's actions' or 'here are my five pages of notes, help me polish them into an essay.'

points.h: Detecting AI is theoretically impossible, but practically sufficient
points.body: In 2023, Max asked research friends whether AI text could be detected; the unanimous answer was 'impossible, don't try, and models will only get stronger.' Pangram's response was to abandon theoretical counterexamples (like 'have ChatGPT paraphrase any text to disprove it') and focus only on practical scenarios: when the input information is less than the output, that's a trace of AI involvement—Bryan calls it word inflation. This definition also explains why early Yelp/Amazon fake reviews didn't become a breakthrough: platforms felt AI reviews were only 3% and not worth worrying about.

points.h: Catching AI isn't about em dashes; it's about synthetic mirroring
points.body: Pangram is a classifier model, not a surface-level rule detector like em dash checkers. The approach: take an open-source LLM, replace its 'predict next token' head with a classification head that outputs a 0-15 AI involvement score. Training data is built via 'synthetic mirroring': take human-written articles, have an LLM compress them into prompts (like 'write a 200-word piece covering these three points'), then feed those to random frontier models to get a human/AI pair on the same topic. A second layer uses editing prompts for clause-level annotation: unchanged text is human, modified text is AI-assisted, and entirely new sentences are AI-generated.

points.h: A detector's lifeline is false positive rate, not accuracy
points.body: Pangram 4 has a false positive rate of about 1 in 24,000, measured by running millions of pre-2022 documents (when AI ghostwriting was nearly impossible); the false negative rate is about 1 in 300, measured by regenerating with frontier models from real user prompts in WildChat. Not perfect, but the direction is right. Bryan's experience is that false positives are extremely low, and that's the lifeline for whether the product can be taken seriously. Pangram 4's step change came from switching from a 512-token window to token-level output: even a fully human-written document with two AI sentences in the middle can be pinpointed word by word.

points.h: Detectors don't need to be 100% accurate; they just need to make cheating costly
points.body: Max says education is a huge market, and this year is the first time people realize 'a truly usable AI detector exists.' The product logic isn't 100% precision but creating friction on the shortcut—making 'throwing homework at AI' go from zero cost to some cost, so students will take the next easiest path, which is doing it themselves. This judgment applies equally to enterprise contexts: Oxide's hiring is a writing-intensive process, and LLM-generated boilerplate in 'why do you want to join Oxide' essays is instantly recognizable; the detector just makes it explicit.

points.h: 'False positive' sob stories online are mostly astroturf ads
points.body: Max distinguishes two types of opposition. One group genuinely wishes detectors didn't exist: it allows the AI text they produce professionally to be authoritatively identified. The other is the humanizer ecosystem's marketing: these tools claim to rewrite AI text to fool Turnitin and Pangram, selling to students caught with AI homework; they typically also include an 'AI detector' that first flags your text as AI, then sells the rewriting service. Many Reddit posts about 'teacher falsely flagged my essay as 76% AI, gave me a zero' are astroturf for this lead generation—run them through Pangram and they're all AI-written.

points.h: Stronger models haven't made detection harder; they've made it easier
points.body: Asked if they're forever chasing frontier models, Max gives a counterintuitive take: two things happen simultaneously—models get smarter, but post-training that repeatedly teaches 'correctness' and preferences narrows the output distribution far more than in the GPT-2 era. GPT-2 tried to mimic the full distribution of human output; today's models only give 'correct' tokens, not what an ordinary person would say. His and Oxide's three-person intuition aligns: new models speak with a 'strangely erudite' flavor, and detection hasn't gotten harder—it's gotten easier.

points.h: The next battleground is how much the human actually input
points.body: Pangram can already guess the model family internally: the probe's top-1 accuracy is 90%, but productization would need to reach 98%. Further out is 'reverse Pangram'—inferring what prompt might have generated a text and how much context the model had: two bullet points or fifteen? This dimension's information content would characterize Druckenmiller's op-ed completely differently—giving five pages of notes to polish is collaboration; giving five bullet points to expand is ghostwriting. The next detection battleground isn't 'did you use AI?' but 'how much did the human actually input?'
